title: Rau Muống Xào Tỏi
subtitle: stir-fried water spinach with garlic
excerpt: Rau muống xào tỏi is a Vietnamese stir-fry of water spinach with masses of garlic and a splash of fish sauce. It is quick, simple, and one of the most popular vegetable dishes in Vietnam. This recipe serves 4 as a side dish.
sourceNotes: Water spinach stir-fried with garlic is one of the most common everyday dishes in Vietnam. It appears on nearly every home table and in every restaurant as part of a family meal.

glossaryTerms.definition: Water spinach, also called morning glory or kangkong. It has hollow stems and dark green leaves. The stems remain slightly crunchy even when cooked.
The smoky, slightly charred flavour produced by cooking in a very hot wok. In Vietnamese stir-fries, this intense heat is what makes vegetables taste restaurant-quality at home.

content.text: Rau muống xào tỏi is a 5-minute stir-fry of
rau muống
water spinach with garlic.
The wok must be very hot to get good
wok hei
flavour.
This recipe serves 4 as a side dish.
If water spinach is hard to find, regular spinach or ong choy from an Asian supermarket both work well. Use the same method.
What you need

items.prepNote: use water spinach (rau muống), cut into 8 cm lengths

content.text: Method
Wash the water spinach and shake off as much water as you can. Cut into 8 cm lengths, keeping the stems and leaves together.
Heat the wok over the highest possible heat until smoking. Add the oil and heat for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and any chilli. Stir-fry for 20 to 30 seconds until fragrant and just starting to turn golden.
Add the water spinach all at once. Toss and stir vigorously for 2 to 3 minutes until wilted and bright green.
Add the fish sauce and toss for 30 more seconds. Taste and season if needed.
Transfer to a plate immediately. Serve hot with steamed rice and other dishes.

attrs.symptom: The spinach is watery and soggy.
attrs.cause: The wok was not hot enough, causing the spinach to steam rather than fry.
attrs.fix: Get the wok smoking before adding oil. Do not add too much spinach at once - it lowers the pan temperature.

attrs.symptom: The garlic burns before the spinach is cooked.
attrs.cause: The garlic was left in the hot oil too long before adding the greens.
attrs.fix: Have the spinach ready to add the moment the garlic starts to turn golden. The greens cool the pan down quickly.

attrs.symptom: The stems are tough and the leaves are overcooked.
attrs.cause: The stems and leaves were cooked together from the start without separating.
attrs.fix: Add the stems to the wok first and cook for 1 minute before adding the leafy tops.

content.text: Where this dish lives
Rau muống is one of the most commonly eaten vegetables in Vietnam.
It grows wild along waterways and is cultivated in paddy fields and ponds across the country.
Every Vietnamese family eats it stir-fried with garlic as part of a regular family meal.
It is cheap, widely available, and cooks in minutes.
The dish appears on the table at nearly every family dinner in Vietnam.
